The software provides an end-to-end workflow from raw spectral import through to supervised and unsupervised machine-learning analysis within a single graphical interface.

The application supports interactive inspection of individual spectra alongside batch processing of complete datasets. Preprocessing steps include spectral alignment to a reference peak, Extended Multiplicative Scatter Correction (EMSC) for background removal, two-stage baseline correction, Savitzky-Golay smoothing, spectral truncation, optional spectral region zapping, and several normalisation strategies including Amide I peak normalisation, total area normalisation, and user-selected peak normalisation. Every processing stage can be visualised independently, allowing users to assess the effect of each operation on the spectrum.

Processed datasets can be saved and reloaded, enabling reproducible analysis workflows without repeating computationally intensive preprocessing steps. All processing parameters are stored alongside the processed data to ensure traceability and reproducibility.

The application includes a suite of multivariate analysis tools. Principal Component Analysis (PCA) is implemented for dimensionality reduction, variance analysis, loading interpretation, and score visualisation. Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection (UMAP) is provided for unsupervised visualisation of high-dimensional datasets using either raw processed spectra or PCA-reduced representations.

For supervised classification, the software implements a PCA-LDA workflow with k-fold cross-validation. Classification performance is assessed using cross-validated confusion matrices and fold-specific performance metrics. LDA score visualisation is based exclusively on held-out validation data, ensuring that displayed class separation reflects model generalisation rather than training performance. Associated LDA loadings facilitate interpretation of the spectral features driving class discrimination.

The application was designed specifically for Raman spectroscopy datasets but can be readily applied to other vibrational spectroscopy modalities that require systematic preprocessing and multivariate analysis. By integrating preprocessing, quality control, dimensionality reduction, classification, and visualisation into a single interface, RamanPreprocessing provides an accessible platform for both expert spectroscopists and new users seeking reproducible Raman data analysis workflows.

References:
For the EMSC algorithm, this was adapted from the implementation by:
Martens, H., & Stark, E. (1991). Extended multiplicative signal correction and spectral interference subtraction: New preprocessing methods for near infrared spectroscopy. Journal of Pharmaceutical and Biomedical Analysis, 9(8), 625-635.

Baseline subtraction is performed using the iterative minimum-envelope algorithm implemented in f_baseline_corr, developed at the Hannoversches Zentrum für Optische Technologien (HOT), Leibniz Universität Hannover, by M. Mazurenka and C. Suhr based on earlier work by M. Koch.
